Chronology 7 — Jesus: Birth, Mission, Crucifixion

Here the two texts are simultaneously closest and furthest apart: a remarkable shared portrait of Jesus' person, broken by one head-on historical contradiction.

Striking agreement

BibleQur'an
Virgin birthMatt 1; Luke 1Q 19:16–22; 3:47
Title "Messiah"Yesal-Masih (Q 3:45)
Miracles by God's powerYesQ 3:49; 5:110
Healed/raised the deadYesQ 3:49 ("by God's leave")
Sinless / pureYesQ 19:19 ("a pure boy")
Word/Spirit from GodJohn 1Q 4:171
Honoured virgin motherLuke 1Q 19 (whole sura)
Will return before the endYesIslamic tradition; Q 43:61

No other figure is shared in such high relief. The Qurʾan's nativity is vivid in its own right: Mary withdraws, the palm tree and stream, and the infant speaks from the cradle — "peace be upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive" (Q 19:29–33). (Note: the clay-bird miracle, Q 3:49/5:110, parallels the apocryphal Infancy Gospel of Thomas, and the cradle-speech the Arabic Infancy Gospel — academic literary observations, recorded neutrally, cutting no deeper than the Genesis–Gilgamesh parallel in cap. 12.)

Conversely, the Bible has Jesus make the claims the Qurʾan denies — "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), "before Abraham was, I AM" (John 8:58), "It is finished" at the cross (John 19:30), and the Supper's self-interpretation "this is my blood… for the forgiveness of sins" (Matt 26:28). The Qurʾanic Jesus disclaims exactly this (Q 5:116–117). That is the cap. 05 seam and is not re-argued here.

The two head-on collisions

1. Deity and sonship — already adjudicated

The Qur'an explicitly denies Jesus' deity and divine sonship (Q 4:171; 5:72–75; 19:88–93). This is the cap. 05 / cap. 09 seam, not re-litigated here.

2. The crucifixion — a factual contradiction

  • Bible: Jesus was crucified, died, was buried, and rose — the center of the message, in all four Gospels and the earliest creed (1 Cor 15:3–8, datable to within a few years of the events).
  • Qur'an: "they did not kill him nor crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them… God raised him to Himself" (Q 4:157–158). Mainstream Muslim reading: a substitution / it only seemed so.

This is the one place the arbiter's own evidentiary rules (Methodology §1: datable physical/historical evidence outranks later tradition) yield a clear lean — on the narrow historical question only:

  • The crucifixion under Pilate is regarded by secular and critical historians (Ehrman, Crossan, Sanders, Lüdemann) as one of the most securely established facts of ancient history: multiply attested (all four Gospels + Paul), early (1 Cor 15:3–8 is a creed within a few years), externally noted by Tacitus (Annals 15.44) and the minimal authentic core of Josephus, and meeting the criterion of embarrassment (a crucified messiah was a scandal no movement would invent).
  • The Qurʾanic denial appears ~600 years later with no earlier documentary or historical corroboration, and its meaning is debated even within Islam.

So, strictly as a past event — "was Jesus crucified?" — the evidence strongly favours the Bible's claim. This is a verdict about the event, not about its salvific meaning, which is out of remit.

The Qur'an's own text on Jesus' death is not simple

Symmetry and accuracy require resisting the popular slogan "Islam says Jesus never died." The Qurʾanic data is internally complex:

  • Q 4:157–158 — not killed, not crucified; "*it was made to appear so (shubbiha lahum)"; God raised him*.
  • Q 19:33 — Jesus speaks of "the day I die".
  • Q 3:55 — "*I will take you (mutawaffīka) and raise you to Me" — tawaffā normally means cause to die*.
  • Q 4:159 — the People of the Book "will believe in him before his death".

Classical and modern Muslim readings therefore diverge: substitution (someone else crucified — the majority classical view), the swoon/no-real- death view, "raised then dies later (at the second coming)", and the Ahmadī natural-death position. The honest statement is: the Qurʾan denies the crucifixion specifically, but does not cleanly deny Jesus' death as such, and Muslim exegesis is itself unsettled. The contradiction with the Bible is therefore about the crucifixion as the mode and meaning of death, not a simple "died vs. never died".

Resurrection — flagged, not scored

The death is near-certain historically. For the resurrection, even skeptical scholars generally grant a bedrock: the disciples sincerely believed they saw the risen Jesus, and the movement exploded from that conviction. What explains it — bodily resurrection (Wright, Habermas, Licona), visionary/hallucination, cognitive-dissonance, or legend (Lüdemann, Ehrman) — is contested historically and theologically. The arbiter presents the range and forces no verdict on the resurrection itself (Methodology §5).

Arbiter verdict — Jesus

Present. Extensive shared Christology of the person (virgin birth, Messiah, miracles, sinlessness, return); flat contradiction on deity and on the crucifixion as event.

Weigh.

  • Strong shared core: the agreed material is large and specific — not vague overlap.
  • Decisive on the event: by the dossier's own neutral evidentiary standard, the historicity of the crucifixion is exceptionally well attested; the denial is late and uncorroborated.
  • Out of remit: the meaning of the death (atonement) and the resurrection as a supernatural claim are not scored.

Judge. This is the one chapter where the neutral historical method produces a clear lean: on the bare factual question "was Jesus crucified?", the evidence favours the Bible and runs against Q 4:157 — explicitly limited to the historical event, and with the added precision that the Qurʾan's broader text on Jesus' death is internally complex and exegetically unsettled, so the firm conflict is specifically over the crucifixion, not over whether Jesus ever died. On who Jesus is (God or prophet) and what the death achieves (atonement or nothing to atone — the cap. 11 seam), the arbiter rules only that each system is internally coherent and that the truth of those claims is out of scope. The seam reaches its sharpest point: the Fall created the need, and here the texts split on whether the need was met — and even on whether the defining event happened.
